In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, both occurrences appearing in Song of Solomon 8:11. Because the available wording identifies the name but does not provide a fuller lexical definition, its precise significance must be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

e.t: This Hebrew noun names “sardius.” It refers to a particular precious stone and is used as a noun when that stone is mentioned. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times: twice in Exodus and once in Ezekiel. The word therefore identifies the stone itself, while the surrounding passage determines what is being said about it in each occurrence.

This Hebrew verb means “forth,” expressing movement or action proceeding outward. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Psalm 144:6. Because the word occurs only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence belongs to the passage’s context. Its basic function is to mark something moving or being sent forth rather than to name a person, object, or quality.

Geba is a place name, referring to a location mentioned in the Old Testament. Its approved rendering is “Geba,” and it functions as a proper name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This Hebrew word occurs 18 times in 18 Old Testament verses, from Joshua through Zechariah. The surrounding passage identifies what is happening at Geba in each occurrence.

This Hebrew verb means “cut,” describing the act of making a physical incision or severing something. In the Old Testament, it occurs eight times across eight verses, so its basic sense is established by repeated use rather than by a single passage. The word can describe cutting oneself, as well as cutting or gathering people together in contexts where bodily action is involved. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “pride,” expressing an elevated view of oneself that places personal honor or status above proper humility. It functions as a name for this inward attitude rather than as an action word. The term occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Job and Jeremiah. Its repeated rendering as “pride” supports this central sense, while its uses should be understood through the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a “fleece”—the woolly covering obtained from a sheep. It functions as a noun for the fleece itself, whether spoken of as something given from a flock or as material associated with cutting or gathering. It occurs four times in the Old Testament, including passages involving sheep, a king’s vision, and imagery connected with freshly cut growth. Its central idea remains the fleece as an object connected with sheep and shearing.

The word means “abhor.” It functions as a verb, expressing an action directed toward someone or something. Across its ten Old Testament occurrences, this word describes the act named by that meaning, rather than a person, place, or object. It appears in Leviticus, Jeremiah, Job, 2 Samuel, and Ezekiel. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the specific object and force must be read from each passage.

This Hebrew word expresses “joining.” It points to the act or condition of being joined, so it describes closeness between people or things rather than treating them as separate. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with each occurrence appearing in a different verse. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence.

This Hebrew verb means “seek.” It describes the action of deliberately turning toward or pursuing something, especially in a way that calls for active attention rather than passive awareness. In the Old Testament, it can function with God as the one sought, expressing a person’s directed response toward him. The word occurs 165 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its precise force depends on the sentence and object connected with it.

e.t: The Hebrew word “Hodijah” is a personal name. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object, so its role is to name someone in the passage. The name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament data, both in Nehemiah: Nehemiah 8:7 and Nehemiah 9:5. Its precise significance in either verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a person’s name.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Haman,” referring to the man named throughout Esther. It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 54 times, all in Esther, where it appears in scenes involving speech, royal commands, and bowing or worship. The name first appears in Esther 3:1 and continues through Esther 9:24, consistently identifying the same person in the narrative.

This Hebrew word expresses an action attributed to the LORD. It occurs twice in the Old Testament corpus, both times in Psalms: Psalm 145:14 and Psalm 146:8. In the Psalm 146:8 relationship, the LORD is identified as the subject performing this action, so the word describes something God does. The available material does not provide an explicit English meaning or enough verse text to state the action more precisely without guessing. Its exact sense should therefore be understood from the surrounding wording of each psalm.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to the ears, the bodily organs by which people hear. It can also function in expressions involving receiving spoken words or attending to commands, connecting the physical ear with the act of listening. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 188 times, showing that it is a common word for ears and hearing. Its use appears in speech-related settings and alongside commandment themes, while its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word refers to “Hammon,” a proper name rather than a general description or action. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, and both occurrences are rendered Hammon. Because no explicit definition or verse text is available here, the safest understanding is simply the name itself. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding context, but the word consistently functions as the name Hammon.

This Hebrew word functions to indicate direction or destination, expressed by the meaning “into.” It connects an action with what lies within or toward its destination, helping show where that action is directed. The word occurs 22 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 21 verses. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words and passage, but its basic contribution is to mark the direction or destination associated with an action.

This Hebrew noun refers to “jewels,” valuable decorative objects. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Song of Solomon 1:10. The available rendering identifies the word as “jewels,” giving the clearest ordinary meaning for this rare term. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself denotes precious adornments rather than an action or quality.

This Hebrew verb expresses the action of making something “bare,” or leaving it without its covering. It can describe exposing a person or object, and its exact force depends on what is being acted upon in the sentence. The word occurs 11 times in the Old Testament, including passages where something is exposed or laid open. Its use is therefore concrete and action-oriented rather than a description of a permanent condition.

e.t: Jair is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Jair.” It identifies people rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears nine times in the Old Testament corpus and is associated with several individuals or references across Israel’s history, including accounts connected with territory and genealogy. Its role is therefore primarily naming a person; the surrounding passage is needed to determine which Jair is meant in a particular verse.

Jedaiah is a Hebrew personal name, used to identify a particular person rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it occurs twice: once in 1 Chronicles 4:37 and once in Nehemiah 3:10. The name is rendered “Jedaiah” in both occurrences, so that name is the supported meaning here. Its specific historical significance belongs to the surrounding passages, not to the name’s ordinary lexical function.

Jamin is a personal name used to identify people in the Old Testament. In this Hebrew corpus, it appears six times, each in a separate verse, and English renderings consistently preserve it as “Jamin.” Its normal function is identification rather than description of an action or quality. Because the name is applied to more than one person, the surrounding passage determines which Jamin is intended. It appears in genealogical and community-related passages across the Hebrew Scriptures.

This Hebrew word refers to “Ismachiah,” functioning as a person’s name rather than describing an action or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 2 Chronicles 31:13. The English renderings preserve the same name, so its ordinary use is to identify an individual. It is not presented here as a general vocabulary term with a broader definition.

e.t: This word means “Jethro,” the personal name of Moses’ father-in-law. It functions as a proper name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs nine times, all in Exodus, where it identifies the same person across references to Moses, his family, and his response to God’s work. The name also appears in passages involving spoken communication and blessing, but those settings do not change its basic meaning as a personal name.

e.t: This Hebrew verb means “lie,” describing the act of lying or making a false claim. It is used of what a person says and can function as the predicate of a sentence. The word occurs 18 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages involving human speech and claims about what will happen. Its basic sense remains the same whether the subject is a person or another being. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word refers to “Pleiades,” the named group of stars. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job and Amos. The word appears when Scripture speaks of the heavenly bodies as part of God’s ordering and governing of the skies, though its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage. It is found in Job 9:9, Job 38:31, and Amos 5:8.

This Hebrew word means “like,” marking a comparison between one thing, person, or situation and another. It points to resemblance or correspondence, helping a sentence say that something is comparable to something else. It occurs 142 times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, so it serves as a broadly used comparison word rather than naming one specific object or idea. Its exact force is determined by what is being compared in each sentence.

This Hebrew word is an interrogative term that asks about “manner”—how something is or was done. It functions as a question word rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 10 times, each in a separate verse, so its precise force is determined by the sentence in which it appears. Its recognized meaning clue is “manner,” and no broader set of meanings should be assumed from the available information.

This word means “write”: to put words, instructions, records, or descriptions into written form. It can function as an action commanded of a person or as a description of something that has been recorded. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 227 times, showing a broad use for preserving information, communicating instructions, and documenting matters. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew verb means “gather,” describing the act of collecting things together, often from a place where they are scattered or available. It can also appear as “gathered” when describing the completed action. In the Old Testament, it is used 37 times, including instructions to gather food, references to gathering crops, and commands concerning what remains in a field. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

This Hebrew word means “void,” referring to an empty, desolate condition. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Nahum 2:10, and its normal function is as a noun describing the state of something reduced to emptiness. The word does not by itself explain the cause or full significance of that condition; those details belong to the surrounding passage. Its single occurrence makes “void” the clearest supported meaning for understanding the word.

“Medes” refers to the people of Media, an ancient kingdom mentioned in the Old Testament. This Hebrew word functions as a people-group name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra and Daniel. The passages associate the Medes with the Persian period and with royal laws that were treated as binding. Thus, the word identifies a historical people who formed part of the kingdoms and political powers encountered in those accounts.

This Hebrew word is a rare term whose ordinary English meaning cannot be stated confidently from the available lexical information. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 21:10. In that passage, it functions as the object connected with hearing and declaring, but those relationships do not by themselves establish what the word means. Its precise sense therefore requires the actual verse wording and surrounding context rather than a confident gloss or expanded definition.

It should therefore be read as a person’s name, not expanded into a separate descriptive meaning.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a “censer,” a vessel used in the worship service. It may appear in the plural as “censers.” The word occurs 22 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in passages describing priestly or sanctuary service. It is associated with objects that were made, given, commanded, and carried, including the service described in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers. Its exact significance in any individual verse depends on that passage’s surrounding text.

The word is the personal name “Machbanai,” identifying a person rather than describing an object, action, or quality. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 12:13, so its meaning is chiefly its identifying function as a name. No broader descriptive definition or related scriptural usage is available here; therefore, it should be understood simply as the name Machbanai in that passage.

This Hebrew word refers to someone who is poor—lacking wealth or material resources. It describes a condition of poverty rather than naming a specific person or place. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it occurs four times, all in Ecclesiastes, where English translations consistently render it as “poor.” Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a person of limited material means.

This Hebrew word occurs 18 times in the Old Testament corpus, appearing from Leviticus through Zechariah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains a fountain as a source of flowing provision.

This Hebrew word means “myrrh,” the name of a substance mentioned in the Old Testament. It occurs 12 times across 11 verses, from Exodus through Song of Solomon, with most occurrences in Song of Solomon. The word names a thing rather than an action, so it functions as a concrete noun in its sentences. Its precise significance in any verse depends on that passage’s wording and context.

In the Old Testament, it occurs four times, describing something associated with ordered service, protection, or obedience. Its references span 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, and Isaiah, showing use in both royal or military settings and broader descriptions of submission to authority.

In the Old Testament, the word is used 44 times, including descriptions of leaders over Israel and rulers whose position is connected with God’s appointment or command. Its central idea is authority exercised in a governing role, rather than merely personal prominence.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “fallow,” functioning as a noun for ground left uncultivated or unplowed. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Hosea. Its wording belongs to agricultural language and describes land in relation to cultivation. In Hosea, it is connected with actions such as seeking, sowing, and receiving rain, reinforcing its place in farming imagery rather than referring to a person or abstract quality.

This Hebrew word describes something as “pleasant”—agreeable, attractive, or enjoyable in character. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 17:10, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated scriptural examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea is something pleasing rather than harsh, burdensome, or undesirable.

This Hebrew verb describes being “alienated,” expressing a condition of estrangement or rejection. It functions in a sentence as an action or state affecting a person or relationship, rather than naming an object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Ezekiel 23:18, 23:22, and 23:28. Its repeated rendering points to a consistent sense across its limited usage, while the surrounding passage determines the immediate situation.

This Hebrew word refers to a “warrior”—someone identified by a military or fighting role. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 9:5. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context. Its basic meaning remains a person associated with warfare or battle, rather than a general description of every person or leader. This is the only recorded Hebrew-corpus occurrence for the word.

This Hebrew word is the name “Eden,” referring to a named place or region rather than describing an ordinary action or quality. It appears three times in the Old Testament, in 2 Kings 19:12, Isaiah 37:12, and Ezekiel 27:23. In each recorded rendering, it is preserved as “Eden.” The word’s precise geographical or contextual significance depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function is as a proper place-name.

This Hebrew word means “chamber,” identifying a physical place. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Daniel 6:10. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. It is best understood as a location term, not as a description of a person, action, or quality. The word therefore points to a chamber as a distinct place within the setting described by the passage.

“Prisoners” refers to people held in captivity or confinement. This Hebrew noun identifies those who are not free and are under the control or restraint of others. It occurs four times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, in Psalm 79 and three passages in Isaiah. In these uses, it functions as the person or people affected by actions directed toward them, rather than naming the action itself. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “ashes,” referring to the powdery remains left after something has burned. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Exodus 9, where it functions as an object—the material being taken or used. Its basic meaning is therefore concrete and physical rather than a broad symbol or abstract idea. The surrounding passage is needed to explain its particular significance in each occurrence.

The word means “divided,” describing something separated into distinct parts rather than joined as one. It is a Hebrew term found once in the Old Testament, with its only recorded occurrence at Daniel 2:41. The basic idea is a lack of complete unity: what is described is partitioned or composed of separate portions. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on being divided rather than remaining whole.

The word occurs 23 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Nehemiah. Scripture repeatedly places the Perizzites among the peoples encountered by Israel, including in commands and statements about the land. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on that passage’s context.

Aphek is a Hebrew place-name, rendered “Aphek” in English. It identifies a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The name occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in passages connected with Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, and other historical settings. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding account and which location is intended. The word itself functions as a proper name for that place.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “food”—something prepared, carried, or supplied for people to eat. It can describe what travelers take with them, what is distributed to others, or what is needed before setting out. The word occurs 12 times in the Old Testament, showing its ordinary use for edible supplies in different situations. Its precise force in a particular verse comes from how the surrounding sentence presents that food.

This Hebrew word refers to “wafers,” a kind of food. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Exodus 16:31, and the English renderings agree on this meaning. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that sentence cannot be described further. Its basic sense is therefore a food term naming wafers, rather than an action, quality, or person.

This Hebrew word means “ancient,” describing something belonging to a very distant past rather than something recent or new. It functions as a descriptive word, marking an object or reality by its age or long-standing character. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Judges 5:21. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage depends on its context, but its central sense is clear: ancient.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “nest,” referring to a bird’s dwelling or resting place. It is used throughout the Old Testament and appears 13 times, including passages that speak of birds, shelter, and a settled dwelling. The word can function as the object of actions such as taking, lying in, or stirring a nest. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word means “stubbornness.” It names a resistant, unyielding quality rather than an action. In its one Old Testament occurrence, it functions as a noun in Deuteronomy 9:27. The word describes a settled condition that can characterize a people, helping explain why Moses appeals to God not to regard Israel’s stubbornness. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a will that resists correction or direction.

This Hebrew verb means “multiply.” It describes people, animals, possessions, or other things becoming greater in number. It can also describe the process of making something more numerous, so its basic idea concerns increase in quantity rather than a particular object or person. The word appears 235 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that this is a broadly used expression for becoming or becoming greatly more. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being multiplied and the surrounding sentence.

e.t: In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word refers to “savour,” especially in connection with something offered or given. It commonly appears alongside sacrificial offerings, including those described in Exodus and Leviticus, and it can also occur in broader passages about what is presented before God. The word occurs 58 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with many uses in Numbers and Leviticus. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “rough,” describing something uneven rather than smooth. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 40:4. Its meaning points to a rugged or irregular surface, though the precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording. The word functions as a description of physical terrain, helping portray what is uneven being changed or made level. This is its only recorded occurrence in the Hebrew corpus.

This Hebrew word means “shepherd,” referring to a person who tends and leads sheep. It functions as a noun naming the one responsible for a flock. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it occurs 11 times, including passages involving human shepherds and the shepherding role associated with Israel’s ruler. Its usage can therefore describe both ordinary care of sheep and the recognized responsibility of guiding and caring for others.

This word refers to the “Shuhamites,” a named people group in the Hebrew Old Testament. It functions as a group designation rather than a general description or action. The word occurs twice, both times in Numbers 26, where it identifies the same people group in the genealogical listing. Its precise significance in each verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic reference remains the Shuhamites. [p03:word:hebrew:H7749:renderings] [p03:word:hebrew:H7749:occurrences]

This Hebrew word means “cursed.” It describes a person, people, or thing as being placed under a curse, and it can function as the sentence’s predicate—what is said about someone or something. It appears 63 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Malachi. Its use includes statements about individuals, nations, and objects, so the surrounding sentence determines precisely who or what is described as cursed.

e.t: Shittim is a proper name used for a place in the Old Testament. It is rendered “Shittim” and functions as a geographical name rather than a description or action. The word occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Numbers, Joshua, Joel, and Micah. Its precise significance in any one passage comes from that passage’s surrounding context, but its ordinary lexical role is to identify Shittim by name.

Shalmai is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it appears twice: once in Ezra 2:46 and once in Nehemiah 7:48. The available English rendering presents it as “Shalmai,” so its ordinary lexical sense is best stated as the person’s name, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific identification.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “delight,” expressing something cherished as a source of pleasure or deep satisfaction. It occurs nine times in the Old Testament corpus, including several uses in Psalm 119 and appearances in Proverbs, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. The word can describe what a person finds pleasing and precious, and it may also identify the object of such delight. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word describes something bare or high, especially a raised or exposed place. Its two main biblical renderings are “bare” and “high,” so the surrounding sentence determines which aspect is emphasized. It occurs ten times in the Old Testament, including passages where it serves as the setting or object associated with speech and movement. The word therefore points to elevated, open ground rather than an abstract quality.

This Hebrew word refers to “bleatings”—the audible cries or sounds of animals. It is a concrete noun for animal sounds rather than a human statement or abstract idea. In the Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, in Judges 5:16 and Jeremiah 18:16. Its normal sense is an animal cry, while the surrounding verse determines how that sound functions in the sentence.

This Hebrew word means “thirty,” the number. It identifies a quantity of thirty and functions as a precise numerical term rather than describing a person, action, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Daniel 6:7 and Daniel 6:12. The word’s basic meaning remains the same wherever it occurs; the surrounding sentence determines what is being counted. Its repeated English rendering as “thirty” confirms this central numerical sense.

This Hebrew word refers to “death,” the end of mortal life. It is a noun describing death as a reality or condition rather than an action. In the Old Testament, it appears only twice, both times in the Psalms: Psalm 79:11 and Psalm 102:20. Its use in these passages places death within prayers addressed to God, while the surrounding wording determines the precise emphasis in each verse.

This Hebrew verb expresses “had,” functioning as an action or state word in a sentence. It occurs 18 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 17 verses. Because the surrounding wording determines how the verb functions in each passage, its precise force can vary by context, but its supported basic sense is the expression of “had.” It appears in passages from Genesis through Isaiah, showing that this verb is used across different periods and settings rather than belonging to one narrow subject.

Agur is a personal name, referring to the individual identified by that name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 30:1, and its English rendering is consistently “Agur.” Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, this entry establishes the name’s lexical function but does not explain the person’s role in that passage.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. As a Hebrew word, it appears once, in Daniel 2:21. The reference identifies where it occurs, but the verse text is not available here, so no specific action, concept, or emphasis should be attached to it from that reference alone. Its precise meaning should therefore be read from the surrounding passage and the way it functions in that sentence.
